title: Operator profiling runbook for multi-model pipelines
author: Priya Nambiar
content:
## Overview

This runbook guides operators and oncall engineers through focused profiling, triage, and mitigation for production inference pipelines that invoke multiple model variants within a single request path (for example: routing -> reranking -> generation). These multi-model pipelines have distinct failure and performance modes due to cross-model kernel contention, KV cache effects, and routing-induced burstiness. The goal is to localize dominant cost/latency contributors, validate fidelity regressions, and recommend safe mitigations.

Audience: SREs, runtime operators, performance engineers, and platform owners.

## When to use this runbook
- Incident symptoms: sudden p95/p99 latency increases, elevated per-token cost, regression alerts from fidelity monitoring tied to specific prompt sets, or increased model swap frequency.
- Pre-launch: run this profiling checklist before enabling new multi-model routing rules or model variants in production.

## High-level profiling objectives
1. Attribute latency to segment (frontend, router, model A, model B, post-processing).
2. Determine kernel-level contention or slow kernel regressions.
3. Measure KV cache hit/miss amplification across chained models.
4. Quantify cost impact (per-token GPU time and dispatched kernel time) and map to SLO risk.

## Signals and dashboards (reference thresholds)
| Signal | Source | Unit | Alert threshold | First action |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| p99 end-to-end latency | metrics.runtime.e2e_latency | ms | > 1200 | Start this runbook |
| p99 per-model inference latency | metrics.runtime.model_latency{model} | ms | > 400 | Inspect kernel traces |
| Kernel stall time | traces.kernel.stall_ratio | % | > 15% | Collect kernel samples |
| KV cache miss amplification | metrics.kvcache.miss_ratio | ratio | increase > 2x baseline | Check routing entropy |
| Per-token GPU time | metrics.gpu.token_time | ms/token | > 0.35 | Run microbenchmarks |
| Failure rate for fallbacks | metrics.runtime.fallback_rate | % | > 1% | Validate model compatibility |

Note: thresholds are a starting point. Tune per-customer/product SLO.

## Preparation steps
1. Notify stakeholders: channel runtime-ops and owning product team, record the incident ID in the investigation notes.
2. Capture a representative traffic window: enable request shadowing to staging or enable request sampling at 5% if live.
3. Ensure tracing level: set TRACE level for router and model-adapter services for a 10 minute window.
4. Reserve GPU profiling quota: request access to profiler nodes and ensure the kernel symbol map is current.

## Data collection checklist
1. Collect full traces for 500 representative requests spanning the bad window (or 10 minutes of high load).
2. Export kernel-level samples (nvprof/NSys or vendor equivalent) for the top 5 impacted GPUs.
3. Pull scheduler and admission logs for the timeframe (slot assignments, preemption events).
4. Gather KV-cache metrics per-shard and per-model for the same window.
5. Snapshot routing decisions and model variant assignment logs for sampled requests.

## Commands and snippets
Use these in the operator sandbox. Replace placeholders.

```bash
# sample trace export (internal cli)
redwoodctl traces export --start 2026-02-14T15:02:00Z --end 2026-02-14T15:12:00Z --service router,model-adapter,dispatcher --out /tmp/trace-window.json

# collect kernel samples from profiler node
ssh profiler-01 sudo nsys profile --trace=nvtx,cuda --output /tmp/prof-report

# query KV cache stats from metrics API
curl -sS "https://metrics.internal/api/query?m=kvcache.miss_ratio&from=2026-02-14T15:02:00Z&to=2026-02-14T15:12:00Z" > /tmp/kvcache.json
```

## Analysis steps and heuristics
1. Decompose end-to-end trace into segments and compute segment p99 contribution. If a single model consumes > 60% of p99, focus there.
2. Inspect kernel traces: look for increased stall_ratio, long memcpy peaks, or unexpected kernel serialization between models. Flag kernels with > 2x baseline latency.
3. Check scheduler logs for back-to-back preemptions or slot thrashing impacting KV cache locality.
4. Correlate routing entropy with KV cache miss amplification. A routing shift that increases model variance often drives cache misses.
5. Run targeted microbenchmarks to reproduce per-model per-shape latency using an isolated GPU: use the sample workload below.

Sample microbenchmark YAML (submit to perf-lab)
| field | value |
|---|---|
| job_name | mm-pbench-{{model}}-seq128 |
| model | model-a-v2,model-b-v1 |
| batch_shapes | [ {batch:1,seq:64}, {batch:1,seq:128} ] |
| duration | 10m |
| trace_level | kernel,scheduler |

## Mitigations (short-term)
- Apply routing rate limit for the upstream service to smooth burstiness.
- Increase admission capacity (if on Dedicated) for the affected pool for 10–30 minutes to reduce queueing.
- Temporarily pin requests to the stable model variant with known lower per-token GPU time.
- Disable non-critical post-processing (rerank stage) to measure its marginal impact.
- If kernel regression is confirmed, rollback the recent kernel or model runtime library change via the kernel rollback playbook.

## Long-term remediation recommendations
- Add model affinity tags to routing decisions to preserve KV cache locality.
- Introduce modeled per-request cost accounting to detect cost regressions alongside fidelity.
- Expand microbenchmark coverage to include chained-model scenarios and publish the benchmark manifests.
- Harden kernel rollout testing to include multi-model chain synthetic traffic.

## Known cross-model failure modes and mitigations
- Kernel serialization: concurrent model kernels serialize due to a scheduling bug. Mitigation: enable per-tenant kernel credit isolation and limit simultaneous kernels per-GPU.
- KV cache thrash: routing entropy leads to cold cache across chained requests. Mitigation: add short-lived prefix caching and warmup hints for high-entropy routes.
- Mismatched quantization paths: model A dispatches a quantized kernel incompatible with model B expectations. Mitigation: enforce variant compatibility matrix in the router.

## Triage decision tree (quick)
1. Is per-model latency the dominant contributor? Yes -> analyze kernel traces. No -> inspect router and network.
2. Are kernel stalls elevated? Yes -> capture kernel sample and escalate to runtime-kernel team. No -> look at queueing and admission.
3. Is KV cache miss ratio increased relative to baseline? Yes -> consider routing affinity and warmup. No -> check microbenchmarks for regression.

## Post-incident steps
1. Create an incident postmortem with timelines, root cause hypothesis, and actions.
2. Add a regression test to the microbenchmark suite that reproduces the identified mode.
3. Schedule a cross-team review if kernel or scheduler change was causal.
4. Update the routing and model-variant SLO documentation if thresholds were insufficient.

## Ownership and escalation
- Primary owner: runtime-ops oncall (runtime-ops rotation).
- Secondary: serving-runtime kernel subteam.
- Escalation: page runtime-sre lead for capacity changes; page runtime-kernel lead for kernel regressions.
